Based on the search results, here's what I found about Blackwell's block-scaled tensor core throughput for MXFP4, NVFP4, and MXFP8:

## Throughput Multipliers

Blackwell's NVFP4 tensor cores run at 2× the throughput of FP8 on the same hardware, and NVFP4 → FP8 → BF16 is a 4× → 2× → 1× throughput stair on B100/B200.

More specifically, the B200 delivers approximately 18,000 sparse FP4 TFLOPS vs 9,000 sparse FP8 TFLOPS, which is a 2x hardware ratio that enables FP4 on Blackwell to produce real throughput gains.

## Block Specifications

For block-scaled configurations:
- MXFP8 extends the FP8 approach with block-level scaling optimized for the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, with each block covering 32 tensor elements
- NVFP4 uses blocks of 16 elements with an E4M3 FP8 scale, compared to MXFP4's 32 elements with power-of-2 E8M0 scaling

## Key Difference

Blackwell also supports NVIDIA's own NVFP4 format, which is known for being more accurate than MXFP4, likely because of its smaller block size, different scaling factor data format, and the two-level quantization method.

# NVIDIA B200 (Blackwell, sm_100) Tensor Cores & CUTLASS for FP32-Equivalent Matmul

## 1. Blackwell 5th-gen tensor cores and the tcgen05 instruction family

**What `tcgen05.mma` is.** `tcgen05` is the PTX instruction family that programs the 5th-generation tensor cores on Blackwell datacenter GPUs (sm_100). `tcgen05.mma` computes `D = A*B + D` (or `D = A*B`), and it is architecturally different from Hopper's `wgmma` in three load-bearing ways:

- **It abandoned registers for the matrix operands.** On Hopper, WGMMA operands/accumulators live in registers across a warpgroup. On Blackwell, "operands now reside in shared memory and Tensor Memory." Specifically, for the MMA: operand A may be in TMEM or SMEM, **operand B must be in SMEM, and the accumulator must be in TMEM** ([Colfax: Writing GEMM Kernels Using Tensor Memory](https://research.colfax-intl.com/cutlass-tutorial-writing-gemm-kernels-using-tensor-memory-for-nvidia-blackwell-gpus/); [SemiAnalysis: Tensor Core Evolution](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/nvidia-tensor-core-evolution-from-volta-to-blackwell)).
- **It is a single-thread instruction.** Blackwell "replaces warp-synchronous MMA with `tcgen05.mma`, a single-thread instruction" — one thread launches the whole MMA, removing warp-level synchronization and the associated register pressure ([SemiAnalysis: Tensor Core Evolution](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/nvidia-tensor-core-evolution-from-volta-to-blackwell); [gau-nernst: tcgen05 for dummies](https://gau-nernst.github.io/tcgen05/)).
- **Tensor Memory (TMEM).** Each SM has a dedicated **256 KB TMEM** (512 columns × 128 lanes × 32-bit), allocated/freed explicitly and accessed via `tcgen05.ld/.st/.cp`. Accumulation happens in TMEM rather than registers ([Colfax: Tensor Memory](https://research.colfax-intl.com/cutlass-tutorial-writing-gemm-kernels-using-tensor-memory-for-nvidia-blackwell-gpus/)).

**The 2x–4x-over-Hopper claim (authoritative, from NVIDIA's CUTLASS docs).** The official CUTLASS documentation states verbatim: *"Blackwell SM100 has 7 new `tcgen05.mma` instructions. These instructions are 2x to 4x faster then [sic] Hopper Architecture's WGMMA instructions."* The breakdown by datatype is ([NVIDIA CUTLASS — Blackwell SM100 GEMMs](https://docs.nvidia.com/cutlass/latest/media/docs/cpp/blackwell_functionality.html)):

| tcgen05.mma path | vs. Hopper |
|---|---|
| Legacy TF32, FP16/BF16, INT8 | **2× faster than Hopper** |
| Mixed-precision F8/F6/F4 (non-block-scaled) | 2× faster than Hopper FP8 |
| Block-scaled F8/F6/F4 | 2× faster than Hopper FP8 |
| Block-scaled **MXF4 / NVF4** | **4× faster than Hopper FP8** |

So the "4×" applies specifically to the new 4-bit block-scaled path, not to TF32/BF16 (those are 2×). An independent microbenchmark study corroborates the latency change: single-instruction `tcgen05.mma` latency is ~11 cycles for all supported tile sizes vs. up to ~128 cycles for Hopper `wgmma` ([Microbenchmarking Blackwell, arXiv:2512.02189](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.02189v1)).

Supported datatypes on the 5th-gen core: **FP64, TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8** ([Colfax](https://research.colfax-intl.com/cutlass-tutorial-writing-gemm-kernels-using-tensor-memory-for-nvidia-blackwell-gpus/); [Microbenchmarking Blackwell](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.02189v1)).

## 2. Datatype support for FP32-ish matmul and the throughput stair

For "FP32-equivalent" matmul the relevant tensor-core inputs are **TF32, BF16, and FP16 (all with FP32 accumulation)**; the low-precision block-scaled formats sit below them. Blackwell adds OCP **microscaling (MX)** formats and NVIDIA's own **NVFP4**:

- **MXFP8** — block of **32** elements, E8M0 (power-of-2) scale ([PyTorch: MXFP8/NVFP4 on Blackwell](https://pytorch.org/blog/faster-diffusion-on-blackwell-mxfp8-and-nvfp4-with-diffusers-and-torchao/)).
- **MXFP4** — block of **32**, power-of-2 E8M0 scale.
- **NVFP4** — block of **16** elements with an **E4M3 FP8 scale** plus a second-level tensor scale; more accurate than MXFP4 because of the smaller block and finer scale format ([zeroentropy: NVFP4](https://www.zeroentropy.dev/concepts/nvfp4/); [NVIDIA: NVFP4 training](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/using-nvfp4-low-precision-model-training-for-higher-throughput-without-losing-accuracy/)).

**The throughput stair (per unit hardware, FP32 accumulate):** `NVFP4/MXFP4 (4×) → FP8/MXFP8 (2×) → BF16/FP16 (1×)`. NVFP4 runs at **2× the throughput of FP8**, and FP4→FP8→BF16 is a **4×→2×→1×** stair on B100/B200 ([SemiAnalysis: Tensor Core Evolution](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/nvidia-tensor-core-evolution-from-volta-to-blackwell)). Relative to the BF16/FP16 line, **TF32 is half** (i.e. TF32 = 0.5× BF16) — confirmed by the absolute numbers in §3 (TF32 dense 1.1 PFLOPS vs BF16 dense 2.25 PFLOPS). So the full stair anchored to BF16=1× is: **FP4 4× / FP8 2× / BF16 1× / TF32 0.5×**.

## 3. Authoritative per-GPU B200 peak numbers — dense vs. sparse

The authoritative source is the **official NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief, Table 3 ("Per Blackwell GPU Specifications" for HGX B200)**. Critically, its footnote reads: **"All petaFLOPS and petaOPS are with Sparsity except FP64 which is dense."** So every tensor number in the table is a **2:4 sparse** figure; **dense = ½**. ([NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief, p.19–20](https://www.aspsys.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/nvidia-blackwell-architecture-technical-brief.pdf) — note this is the per-GPU spec for the B200 inside HGX B200, 1000W TDP, 192 GB HBM3e.)

| Format (per **B200** GPU) | Table value (**sparse**) | **Dense** (½) |
|---|---|---|
| FP4 Tensor Core | 18 PFLOPS | **9 PFLOPS** |
| FP8 / FP6 Tensor Core | 9 PFLOPS | **4.5 PFLOPS** |
| INT8 Tensor Core | 9 PetaOPS | **4.5 PetaOPS** |
| **FP16 / BF16 Tensor Core** | 4.5 PFLOPS | **2.25 PFLOPS** |
| **TF32 Tensor Core** | 2.2 PFLOPS | **~1.1 PFLOPS** |
| FP32 (CUDA core, non-tensor) | — | **80 TFLOPS** (dense) |
| FP64 Tensor Core | — | **40 TFLOPS** (dense) |
| FP64 (vector) | — | **40 TFLOPS** (dense) |

This resolves the common 1.1-vs-1.2 PFLOPS TF32 ambiguity in secondary sources: the NVIDIA brief gives **2.2 PFLOPS sparse → 1.1 PFLOPS dense TF32**. (Some secondary write-ups quote "1.2 PFLOPS dense TF32," e.g. [verda.com](https://verda.com/blog/nvidia-b200-and-b300-gpu-architecture-and-software-stack) / search aggregations — treat the NVIDIA brief's 1.1 as authoritative.)

**The marketing-vs-reality framing for your survey:** NVIDIA's headline "**20 petaFLOPS of FP4**" (and the "9 PFLOPS"/"18 PFLOPS" figures) are the *FP4* and frequently the *2:4-sparse* numbers. For the dense, "FP32-equivalent" matmul that a survey actually cares about:

- **Dense TF32: ~1.1 PFLOPS** (1,100 TFLOPS)
- **Dense BF16/FP16 (FP32 accum): 2.25 PFLOPS** (2,250 TFLOPS)
- **Dense FP8: 4.5 PFLOPS**; **Dense FP4: 9 PFLOPS**

i.e. the dense TF32 reality (1.1 PFLOPS) is **~18×** smaller than the "20 PFLOPS FP4" marketing headline, which is itself ~half-inflated by sparsity. ([NVIDIA Technical Brief](https://www.aspsys.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/nvidia-blackwell-architecture-technical-brief.pdf); FP4 "20 PFLOPS excluding the 2× sparsity gain" framing for the package: [Wikipedia: Blackwell microarchitecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackwell_(microarchitecture)).)

A caveat for precision: the technical brief's per-GPU column is labeled "HGX B200" at 1000W. NVIDIA's own DGX B200 page corroborates the system-level numbers — **144 PFLOPS FP4 sparse / 72 PFLOPS dense across 8 GPUs**, footnoted "*Shown in sparse | dense*" and "*Dense performance is ½ sparse*" — which divides to the same 18/9 PFLOPS FP4 per GPU ([NVIDIA DGX B200](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-b200/)).

## 4. What CUTLASS actually achieves on Blackwell

**Official NVIDIA claim — ~99% of peak.** The CUTLASS documentation/README states that CUTLASS 3.8 extends support to Blackwell SM100 with **"99% peak performance for Tensor Core operations,"** and ships a chart titled *"CUTLASS 3.8's performance as a % of theoretical peak utilization on various input and output data types … on NVIDIA Blackwell SM100"* ([NVIDIA CUTLASS Overview](https://docs.nvidia.com/cutlass/latest/overview.html); [CUTLASS README](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/README.md)). Caveat for your survey: the **per-datatype percentages live only in an SVG chart** (`cutlass-3.8-blackwell-gemm-peak-performance.svg`) that is not machine-readable; the "99%" is the headline summary figure, not a guaranteed per-datatype number. The chart is the figure to cite/screenshot if you need the per-type breakdown.

**Independent absolute BF16 numbers (real B200 silicon).** A from-scratch BF16 GEMM study measured **cuBLAS on B200 at ≈1,551 TFLOPS at M=N=K=8192** and a hand-written kernel reaching **1,408.9 TFLOPS (≈90.8% of cuBLAS)**, climbing to **98.3% of cuBLAS at 4096** and the author's final kernel reportedly **106% of cuBLAS at 8192** ([Paul Chan: Outperforming cuBLAS on B200](https://www.paulwillchan.com/articles/outperforming-cublas-b200)). Useful interpretation: ~1,551 TFLOPS BF16 against a 2,250 TFLOPS dense peak is **~69% of dense peak in practice for cuBLAS at this shape/power** — a realistic high-water mark, well below the marketing "99%" which reflects best-case CUTLASS tiles, not arbitrary shapes.

**Independent low-precision (NVFP4) numbers.** On GPT-OSS-20B MoE GEMMs at large batch, production FP4 kernels reach **~1,117–1,262 TFLOPS (SGLang/FlashInfer/vLLM)**, and **SGLang FP4 ≈ 2.23× SGLang BF16** — confirming the 2×-ish FP4-over-BF16 stair holds in deployed kernels, though achieved FP4 TFLOPS (~1.2 PFLOPS) is far below the 9 PFLOPS dense FP4 peak because MoE GEMMs are small/irregular ([HuggingFace: TFLOPS Gap — FP4 MoE on Blackwell](https://huggingface.co/blog/apsys/blackwell-nvfp4-comparison)).

## Bottom line for the survey

- **Dense, FP32-equivalent B200 peaks (authoritative, per-GPU):** TF32 **1.1 PFLOPS**, BF16/FP16 **2.25 PFLOPS**, FP8 **4.5 PFLOPS**, FP4 **9 PFLOPS**; FP32 CUDA-core **80 TFLOPS**, FP64 **40 TFLOPS** ([NVIDIA Blackwell Technical Brief Table 3](https://www.aspsys.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/nvidia-blackwell-architecture-technical-brief.pdf)).
- **Sparse = 2× these** (the headline "18/9/4.5 PFLOPS" and "20 PFLOPS FP4" marketing numbers are 2:4-sparse and/or FP4).
- **Throughput stair:** FP4 4× / FP8 2× / BF16 1× / TF32 0.5× ([SemiAnalysis](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/nvidia-tensor-core-evolution-from-volta-to-blackwell); confirmed by absolute peaks).
- **tcgen05.mma:** register-free, single-thread, TMEM-accumulated; **2× over Hopper WGMMA for TF32/BF16/INT8, up to 4× for block-scaled FP4** ([NVIDIA CUTLASS docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/cutlass/latest/media/docs/cpp/blackwell_functionality.html)).
- **CUTLASS achieves ~99% of peak** in NVIDIA's best-case chart ([CUTLASS README/Overview](https://docs.nvidia.com/cutlass/latest/overview.html)); independent BF16 reality is **cuBLAS ≈1,551 TFLOPS ≈ 69% of dense peak** at 8192³ ([Paul Chan](https://www.paulwillchan.com/articles/outperforming-cublas-b200)).

**Source-quality notes for an expert reader:** (1) The single most authoritative artifact is the NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief, Table 3 + its sparsity footnote — every dense number above is ½ the table value. (2) The CUTLASS per-datatype percent-of-peak is only published as an SVG chart, so cite the chart, not a text number, for anything finer than the "99%" headline. (3) Colfax's CUTLASS Blackwell tutorial series is the best *mechanism* reference (TMEM, block-scaling, clusters, sub-byte) but deliberately publishes **no** TFLOPS — don't cite it for performance numbers.
